pairs.es: Which letter on the diagram represents the earthquake epicenter?
pairs.en: D — it is the single point where the distance circles from all three seismograph stations (A, B, and C) intersect.

pairs.es: How many seismographs are needed to locate an epicenter, and why?
pairs.en: At least 3. One gives only a circle of possible locations. Two gives two possible points. A third station narrows it to the single intersection point.

pairs.es: Why can't a single seismograph station pinpoint an epicenter on its own?
pairs.en: It can only measure distance (producing a circle of possible locations), not direction. Three stations are needed so all three circles intersect at one point.

pairs.es: Points E, F, and G each lie where exactly two circles overlap. Why is the epicenter NOT at those points?
pairs.en: The epicenter must be confirmed by all three stations. E, F, and G only satisfy two stations each — only point D satisfies all three.

pairs.es: What information does each seismograph station use to calculate its circle's radius?
pairs.en: The time difference between P-wave and S-wave arrivals. A larger gap means the station is farther away, so its circle has a larger radius.

pairs.es: Why can P-waves travel through Earth's core, but S-waves cannot?
pairs.en: S-waves only travel through solids. Earth's outer core is liquid, so S-waves stop there. P-waves can travel through both solids and liquids, so they pass through.

pairs.es: How does distance from the epicenter affect the time between the arrival of P-waves and S-waves?
pairs.en: The farther away, the longer the gap. P-waves are faster and pull ahead of the slower S-waves over longer distances, creating a bigger time difference.

pairs.es: Point A receives both P- and S-waves. What does this tell you about point A?
pairs.en: Point A is close to the epicenter and outside the shadow zone. Both wave types can travel through the solid mantle to reach it without passing through the liquid outer core.

pairs.es: Point B receives only one type of wave. Which type, and why?
pairs.en: Only P-waves. S-waves cannot travel through the liquid outer core, so they never reach point B. P-waves pass through liquids and do arrive.

pairs.es: A seismograph on the far side of Earth records only a P-wave and no S-wave. What does this tell you about its location?
pairs.en: It is in the shadow zone. S-waves were blocked by the liquid outer core; only P-waves could refract through the core and arrive.

pairs.es: If Earth had no liquid outer core, would shadow zones exist? Explain.
pairs.en: No. Shadow zones exist because the liquid outer core blocks S-waves and bends P-waves. A fully solid Earth would let all wave types pass through in all directions.

pairs.es: Why are earthquakes felt more strongly at the epicenter than at locations farther away?
pairs.en: The epicenter is directly above the focus (where energy is released). Closer locations receive more energy before it spreads and weakens with distance.

pairs.es: Which causes more severe surface damage: a shallow-focus or deep-focus earthquake of equal energy? Why?
pairs.en: Shallow-focus. The focus is closer to the surface, so less energy is lost before seismic waves reach the ground. Deeper earthquakes give waves more distance to spread and weaken.

pairs.es: Why do most earthquakes occur along plate boundaries?
pairs.en: Plate boundaries are where plates grind, collide, or pull apart. Friction and stress cause rocks to suddenly slip, releasing stored energy as seismic waves.

pairs.es: Name the three internal layers of Earth shown in Diagram 1, from outermost to innermost.
pairs.en: Mantle → Outer core → Inner core. The mantle is solid rock; the outer core is liquid iron; the inner core is solid iron.

pairs.es: Which labeled station (A, B, C, or D) is in the shadow zone? What is the evidence from Diagram 2?
pairs.en: Station C — its seismogram (IV) shows only a P-wave arrival with no S-wave, which is the signature of the shadow zone on the opposite side of Earth from the epicenter.

pairs.es: Station A is close to the epicenter. Which seismogram (I, II, III, or IV) would it produce?
pairs.en: Seismogram I — P and S waves arrive close together (small time gap) and with large amplitude, because Station A is nearest to the energy source.

pairs.es: Match each seismic station on Diagram 1 (A, B, C, D) to the correct seismogram on Diagram 2 (I, II, III, IV).
pairs.en: A → I (closest: small P-S gap, large amplitude), D → II (moderate distance), B → III (farther: large P-S gap), C → IV (shadow zone: P-wave only, no S-wave).

pairs.es: Seismogram IV shows only a P-wave and no S-wave. Which station recorded it, and why no S-wave?
pairs.en: Station C — it is in the shadow zone directly opposite the epicenter. S-waves cannot pass through Earth's liquid outer core and never arrive at Station C.

pairs.es: Looking at seismograms I, II, and III, what trend do you notice in the P-wave to S-wave time gap?
pairs.en: The gap increases from I → II → III. Each station is progressively farther from the epicenter, giving the faster P-waves more time to pull ahead of the slower S-waves.

pairs.es: Seismogram I shows much larger wave amplitudes than II or III. What does this indicate?
pairs.en: Station A (Seismogram I) is closest to the epicenter. More seismic energy arrives before spreading out, producing stronger ground shaking and larger recorded amplitudes.

pairs.es: Which seismic waves are fastest, and which arrive at a station first?
pairs.en: P-waves (primary waves) are fastest and always arrive first. S-waves (secondary) are slower and arrive second. This time gap is what's used to calculate distance to the epicenter.

pairs.es: If a fifth station recorded P and S waves arriving even closer together than Seismogram I, what would that tell you?
pairs.en: That station would be even closer to the epicenter than Station A — almost directly above the focus, where both wave types arrive nearly simultaneously.
